anatomy.lede: The jaguar is built for power, not speed: a stocky, muscular cat with a broad head, short limbs and, for its size, the strongest bite of the cats measured.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: Jaguars communicate mainly by voice. A typical call is a series of seven to a dozen grunts, more powerful in males than in females.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Jaguars are most active around dawn and dusk, hunting by pouncing on prey from a hidden spot.

hotspots.label: Jaws
hotspots.text: Large, square jaws and prominent cheeks anchor huge muscles. For its size, the jaguar has a greater bite-force capacity than the other cats studied.

hotspots.label: Forelimbs
hotspots.text: Lean bodies and muscular limbs let a jaguar drag heavy prey into cover — one hauled a 34 kg sea turtle 91.5 m.

hotspots.label: Rosettes
hotspots.text: Jaguars' rosettes have distinct spots inside them, unlike the leopard's smaller spots and rosettes.

hotspots.label: Paws
hotspots.text: Large, rounded paws help jaguars swim long distances in rivers and flooded forest.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail measures 70–90 cm, against a head-and-body length of 1.5–1.8 m.

senses.lede: Jaguars are secretive and solitary, and much of their communication is by sound and scent left for others to find.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Females in season call in the early morning and late at night, and males answer and travel to find them. Hunters exploit this by mimicking the call with a hollow gourd.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Jaguars mark their home ranges by spraying urine, leaving droppings in prominent places and scraping trees and the ground.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Two genes involved in optic nerve development, DOCK3 and COL4A5, show signs of positive selection in jaguars, possibly linked to vision.

body.lede: Where other big cats rely on speed or size, the jaguar relies on raw strength concentrated in its head and forequarters.

systems.title: A crushing bite
systems.text: Measurements of jaw muscles from nine cat species found the jaguar had relatively the greatest bite-force capacity, suiting a diet that includes caimans and turtles.

systems.title: A throat built to roar
systems.text: Like other big cats, jaguars cannot purr. They roar instead, thanks to a hyoid bone in the throat attached to a stretchy ligament.

systems.title: Size follows the prey
systems.text: Jaguars in the open Pantanal average 100 kg for males, while those in Honduran forest average 57 kg — perhaps because big hoofed prey is more plentiful in open habitats.

genome.lede: The jaguar genome was first sequenced and published in 2017, alongside comparisons with all the other living big cats.

findings.title: Big cats that interbred
findings.text: The genomes of the Panthera cats show tangled family trees, caused partly by hybridisation between species after they split.

findings.title: Borrowed genes, put to use
findings.text: Some genes that jaguars seem to have picked up through ancient hybridisation also show signs of natural selection within the species, suggesting interbreeding helped big cats adapt.

findings.title: The black jaguar gene
findings.text: Black jaguars carry a small deletion in the MC1R gene, one of at least four separate genetic origins of black coats in the cat family.

mind.lede: The jaguar has long been described as a strict loner. Camera traps and GPS collars are revealing more flexible behaviour.

studies.title: Male partnerships
studies.text: Studies in the Venezuelan Llanos and Brazilian Pantanal recorded 70 cases of cooperation or coalition between males, including joint patrolling and marking. Two coalitions lasted more than seven years.

studies.title: But not hunting together
studies.text: Unlike lions and cheetahs, coalition jaguars spent less time together and were not seen hunting cooperatively. Coalitions were most likely where females lived at high density.

studies.title: An escort out
studies.text: Jaguars have occasionally been seen following people, perhaps to 'escort' them out of their territory. They do not attack humans without provocation.

survival.lede: As top predator of the American tropics, an adult jaguar has no natural enemies — only people.

tactics.title: Ambush from cover
tactics.text: Jaguars stalk on the ground through thick vegetation and pounce from a concealed spot, then drag the kill somewhere secluded to eat.

tactics.title: Hidden in plain sight
tactics.text: Cryptic colouring and secretive habits help jaguars avoid detection by both prey and people.

tactics.title: Up and away
tactics.text: Jaguars climb trees for safety or to hunt, and in flood season may be forced to rest in them.

threats.title: Conflict with ranchers
threats.text: Jaguars occasionally kill cattle and are often shot on sight in ranching areas, despite legal protection.

threats.title: Lost and broken habitat
threats.text: Habitat loss and fragmentation, and overhunting of the jaguar's prey, threaten it across its range.

threats.title: Poaching
threats.text: Jaguars are still illegally killed for their pelts, paws and teeth.

life.lede: Jaguar cubs depend on their mother for almost two years, learning to hunt at her side.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Most births come in the wet season, when prey is plentiful. A litter is usually two cubs, but can be one to four.

stages.name: Newborn cub
stages.text: Cubs are born with their eyes closed and are completely dependent on their mother; their eyes open at about two weeks.

stages.name: Learning to hunt
stages.text: Cubs nurse until 5–6 months old, then begin hunting with their mother, staying with her until they are almost two.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at 12–24 months and males at 24–36 months. Male home ranges usually overlap those of two or three females.

lifespan.value: 11–12 years in the wild; over 20 in captivity
